nodes.name: Run the eval
nodes.notes: Run this before and after touching a threshold. The number on its own is close to meaningless; the number compared against the run before the change is the whole tool.

nodes.name: Every Monday
nodes.notes: Also on a schedule, because the rules are not the only thing that can change the score. An environment variable edited in Coolify, a threshold someone tuned in the editor, a normalisation that quietly changed: all of those move accuracy without a commit to look at.

parameters.query:
-- The previous score for this ruleset, so the run can tell whether it moved.
-- Returns exactly one row even when there is no history, so the comparison
-- downstream does not need to handle a missing node output.
SELECT COALESCE(MAX(accuracy), 0)::float AS previous_accuracy,
       COALESCE((SELECT macro_f1 FROM eval_runs
                 ORDER BY started_at DESC LIMIT 1), 0)::float AS previous_macro_f1,
       COUNT(*)::int AS history
FROM eval_runs
WHERE started_at = (SELECT MAX(started_at) FROM eval_runs);

-- The labelled set, as applications. The column names match what the rules
-- expect, so the rows go straight in with no adapter node between them --
-- and an adapter node is exactly where an eval starts measuring something
-- other than what production runs.
SELECT external_id, email, handle, platform, followers,
       expected_decision, note
FROM golden_set
ORDER BY external_id;

nodes.name: Score with the real rules
nodes.notes: The same workflow 01 calls in production, with the same environment variables. This is the only node in the repository that would be pointless to reimplement here, and it is the reason the ruleset is a sub-workflow at all: an eval that scores a copy of the rules measures the copy.

parameters.query:
INSERT INTO eval_runs
  (ruleset_version, execution_id, total, correct, accuracy, macro_f1,
   per_class, config)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4, $5, $6, $7::jsonb, $8::jsonb)
RETURNING id, accuracy, macro_f1;

nodes.name: Store the score
nodes.notes: Appended, never updated, and stamped with the ruleset version and the thresholds it ran under. Overwriting a single 'current accuracy' row makes every question about direction unanswerable, and direction is the only thing this number is good for.

nodes.name: Regressed?
nodes.notes: A two point drop, not any drop. On 46 cases one row is 2.2 points, so a tighter threshold would fire on normal movement and get muted within a month. The tolerance is a function of the dataset size, and it has to move when the dataset does.

parameters.jsonBody: ={{ JSON.stringify({ text: `screening eval: ${$('Compare').first().json.correct}/${$('Compare').first().json.total} correct, accuracy ${$('Compare').first().json.accuracy}, macro F1 ${$('Compare').first().json.macro_f1}, delta ${$('Compare').first().json.delta}. false accepts ${$('Compare').first().json.false_accepts}, false rejects ${$('Compare').first().json.false_rejects}.` }) }}

nodes.name: Report the score
nodes.notes: The score is reported whether or not it moved. A quality metric you only hear about when it drops is one nobody has a sense of, and without that sense the first drop reads as noise.
